summary:
Texas law restricts trans people's use of sex-separated facilities. Governor Abbott signed the Women's Privacy Act on 22 September 2025 and it took effect on 4 December 2025, requiring restrooms to match the sex recorded on a person's birth certificate and applying to public schools, universities, prisons and Texas government buildings. Facilities face a $25,000 fine for a first violation and $125,000 for subsequent violations. The most recent gender-placements statute reaches prisons only as to restroom use; it does not govern cell assignment or the housing placement of trans prisoners.

Enforcement has begun and has been uneven. On 6 December 2025 Department of Public Safety troopers checked identification at women's restrooms outside the state capitol in Austin, admitting trans women whose identity documents carried female markers. Opponents of the law warn that unclear guidance produces inconsistent and invasive checks, and protests followed at the capitol. The Austin City Council moved to circumvent the law's intent.

The state has also moved against a school district over facility policy. In April 2026 Attorney General Paxton filed a second complaint escalating the state investigation of Austin Independent School District, with a renewed demand for records following a tip-line complaint. It is the first state enforcement inquiry into a school district under a Texas bathroom law.

Gender markers on state documents are closed. House Bill 229, the Women's Bill of Rights, passed in May 2025, signed in June 2025 and effective from September 2025, legally defines female as a person who can biologically produce ova and male as a person who can biologically fertilize ova, requires people with disorders of sex development to select one of two genders with no third-gender recognition, and applies across state statutes, regulations and rules that use gendered terms. It explicitly bans any change of sex on Texas driver's licences and birth certificates. Before that, changing the gender indicator on a birth certificate required a court order, with judicial discretion often referring to WPATH Standards of Care and to a narrative statement from a doctor or therapist that the change was appropriate and in the person's best interest. On 30 January 2025 Governor Abbott separately directed state agencies to recognise only two genders.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned. Senate Bill 14, signed in June 2023, prohibits such care for young people, following a February 2022 opinion from the Attorney General classifying the care as child abuse and directives ordering the Department of Family and Protective Services to investigate parents who facilitate it, with criminal penalties for a knowing failure to report. Five district attorneys publicly refused to apply that position. A temporary injunction issued in March 2022 was reinstated by the Third Court of Appeals after a suit by the ACLU and Lambda Legal on behalf of providers and a family with a 16-year-old transgender girl on puberty blockers. Investigative supervisors testified that cases involving trans children were handled under different rules, with mandatory investigation regardless of evidence and a prohibition on discussing them by email or text.

Texas offers trans people no statewide statutory protection against violence or discrimination. The state hate-crime statute enhances penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity, and it is rarely prosecuted. As of 2021 no state law barred discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations or insurance; Texas courts recognised federal employment protections in March 2021. Municipal ordinances fill part of that gap: Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Plano and San Antonio prohibit gender-identity discrimination in private and public employment, housing and public accommodations, with narrower protections limited to city employment or public accommodations in Denton, El Paso, Arlington, Brownsville, Corpus Christi, Houston, Irving, Lubbock, Mesquite and Waco.

Violence against trans women in Texas is recorded at the highest absolute level of any state: 44 killings between 2008 and 2025, a rate of roughly 7.6 per 100,000 per year on the source's count, which is described as an undercount floor. The ranking is by raw tally, and raw tallies track population size; the per-capita figure is the better comparison across states, and the source provides no per-capita ranking of its own.

A July 2026 legal risk assessment places Texas in the top 'Do Not Travel' tier for adult trans travellers, alongside Florida, Idaho and Kansas, graded state by state across care bans, facility bans and enforcement posture using five years of legislation tracking.

Trans prisoners in Texas have limited access to medically necessary care through the courts. In Gibson v. Collier, Vanessa Lynn Gibson, a transgender woman diagnosed with gender dysphoria and incarcerated by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, was denied gender-confirmation surgery because the agency's treatment policy excluded that procedure. The federal district court rejected the state's immunity defences but ruled against her on the Eighth Amendment claim. The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, finding no deliberate indifference and holding that refusing the surgery was a permissible medical choice, with Judge Barksdale dissenting on summary-judgement procedure.
tangentialFactors:
Texas sits in the most restrictive group of states identified by the July 2026 risk assessment, graded alongside Florida, Idaho and Kansas at the same tier. The comparison reflects each state's own statutes and enforcement posture rather than any shared regional rule.

State policy toward trans students extends beyond facilities. A Parents' Bill of Rights enacted in June 2025 bars school employees from teaching or discussing gender identity, bans LGBT-related student organisations, requires schools to use students' birth names and sex-based pronouns, and expands parental authority over school matters. A DEI law explicitly listing banned school and certain workplace programmes on the basis of sexual orientation has been in effect since 1 September 2025 and is under court challenge.

Other measures sit at various stages. A bill prefiled in November 2022 would broaden the definition of sexually oriented businesses to capture any performance in which a performer uses clothing, makeup or other markers to exhibit gender variance from birth-assigned sex while singing, lip-syncing, dancing or otherwise performing, which would reach transgender performers in any role as well as cisgender portrayals of ambiguous genders, and would criminalise minors attending drag shows. Around fifty bills filed in early January 2023 sought to criminalise youth gender-affirming care, reduce adult access, bar sex-marker changes for minors and restrict sports participation; earlier 2021 bills passed the House 18-13 to revoke the licences of doctors providing blockers to minors. A June 2019 law bars adverse government action against those who support religious organisations that may refuse LGBTQ service, and an October 2020 internal policy permitted social workers to discriminate against LGBT clients. The Trevor Project was removed from state suicide-prevention resources in February 2022.

The Texas legislature has repeatedly failed to repeal its dormant same-sex-only sodomy statute: a 2025 repeal passed the House and died in the Senate, and Texas is one of three states retaining such a law. This provision concerns same-sex conduct and does not, on its face, turn on a person's gender history.
localsOnly:
Trans residents of Texas can no longer alter the sex designation on a state driver's licence or birth certificate, and must be recorded as one of two genders regardless of a diagnosis of a disorder of sex development. The prior route, a court order supported by a clinician's narrative statement, is no longer available.

Residents in the listed cities hold employment, housing and public-accommodation protections on gender identity that the state does not provide. Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Plano and San Antonio carry the broadest set; Denton, El Paso, Arlington, Brownsville, Corpus Christi, Houston, Irving, Lubbock, Mesquite and Waco provide narrower coverage confined to city employment or public accommodations.

There is no statewide recognition of domestic partnerships for couples of any sex. Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, El Paso, Houston and San Antonio provide health insurance to domestic partners of city workers, Travis, El Paso and Bexar Counties permit partner participation, and Pflugerville ISD allows inclusion at full worker cost. An April 2013 Attorney General opinion held that the state constitution bars political-subdivision benefits based on domestic-partnership status, and Houston's 2013 interpretation of a 2014 vote required spousal benefits for legally married same-sex couples.

Any adult in Texas may adopt regardless of sexual orientation, and legally married same-sex couples may adopt jointly and obtain supplemental birth certificates listing both parents, though federally funded adoption agencies may decline clients on religious grounds. The state's hate-crime statute, which does not cover gender identity, is rarely used in either of its covered categories.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Women's Privacy Act or House Bill 229 faces a pending constitutional challenge, and the status of any such litigation, is not established in the sources assembled here.

The outcome of the Austin Independent School District investigation, including any penalty or policy change imposed, had not resolved as of the latest source dated April 2026.

The 44 killings recorded for Texas are an undercount floor on the source's own description, and no per-capita comparison table across states is provided; the 'highest absolute toll' claim is a raw-count ranking and does not by itself establish that Texas is the most dangerous state per resident.

The current scope of Senate Bill 14 after the 2022 injunction litigation, and whether any Texas court has since narrowed or upheld the ban, is unresolved in these sources. The 'Do Not Travel' tier itself is one assessment organisation's methodology rather than a legal finding.

No current figure for hate-crime prosecutions or convictions motivated by gender identity in Texas appears in the sources; the assessment rests on the statutory exclusion of gender identity and the source's statement that the statute is rarely prosecuted.
